utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminary matters were announced. I suggest that we first briefly move into closed sessions in order to allow the witness to come in, and I would like to deal with a matter as well when we are in private session -- closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Witness. Witness, you will give your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you'll give your evidence today under protective measures. The protective measures are pseudonym, image distortion, and voice distortion, which means that we'll not use your own name. We'll address you as "GRM116," that's how we'll call you. No one outside this courtroom will see your face or will hear your voice. You -- there is someone in the courtroom you would know well. His role has been explained to him, and it's not in any way to intervene in the examination. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Witness. Witness, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Can you see the witness, Mr. Stojanovic, sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic, but before we start, we do understand that you brought some papers with you. Would you please put them aside and only consult them after prior consultation. You don't have to give them -- if you just turn them -- yes. Okay. So you shouldn't consult them without having asked permission to do so. Mr. Stojanovic, if are you ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to call up, Your Honours, 65 ter 1D05182 not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, if you could look at the screen before you, there is a document, and without reading anything aloud, would you kindly look at that document and tell us if the personal details indicated there are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could you please look on the right screen. There is the document you should look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- perhaps the usher could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like 65 ter 1D05182 to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MFI'd for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not MFI'd, but admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have been a bit unclear if I understand the interpreters well. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1387, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell the Court what schools you have finished.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: The primary school, the secondary school, high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What jobs did you do before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I worked as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us where and when.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: In Capljina and in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us in which year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a military rank or military training?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav people's army, I did not have a rank; and in Biseri, in the end, they gave me the rank of sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I was in my native town, Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there or did you leave Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: While there were tensions and barricades were put up and while there was a chance of keeping Visegrad, we stay there; however, when the Uzice Corps - provoked by the threat of Mirad Sabanovic [phoen], that he will be blow up the dam - when the Uzice Corps came into town, we left for Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately which month that was in 1992 when you moved to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I believe it was April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just concerned, based on the past transcript that I've reviewed and the nature of the witness's evidence, that we might be getting close to compromising whatever protective measures that he might have been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you've heard the concerns expressed by Mr. Weber. I take it that you'll take care that in -- you'll not be too late in asking for private session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour. I discussed that with the witness yesterday, and we will take care just as we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Gorazde, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question was not answered, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Weber stood up before it could be answered -- oh, it was answered. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, line 10, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us now: After Gorazde where did you go?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: We spent four or five days in Gorazde, and since we were already at war with the Serbs over there in Visegrad, Hadza Afendic, president of the Gorazde municipality, had begun talks about the division of Gorazde into the Serb and the Bosniak parts. We were terrified that this might succeed and one of the men who was us had his own private bus, so we went by that bus to Sarajevo via Sokolac, Han Pijesak, and Golovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Sarajevo, were you at one point engaged into the army?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, when I came there, there were already barricades in Sarajevo. At Pofalici, there was a Bosniak barricade, then a Serbian roadblock. Everything was already prepared for war. It was not long before military units began to be formed, so I had to join one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court how it came that you were inducted into the army when you arrived at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: This relative of mine -- should you tell the name or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, as far as we are concerned, it's not necessary; but if you need to mention him by name, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I don't mind. Everybody knows that in Sarajevo anyway. That relative of mine told me that a new unit was being established around the Presidency by the name of Biseri, that it was a bit safer, I would not be over there where the criminals were, so I agreed and joined. I only later learned that this unit was called Biseri, and I was practically one of the first to join that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court what were the tasks of that unit, Biseri, that you joined.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Our first assignment was to defend the members of the Presidency and the building, that is, to guard the building and all the members of the Presidency and some other VIPs while they were in Sarajevo. That is to say, every member of the Presidency had security provided at home, security during movement, and the building of the Presidency was guarded non-stop. And when Alija was away and in view of the fact that the unit consisted mainly of athletic young men who knew karate and martial-arts - and I was the oldest among them - they were trying to pick out handsome, athletic, young men. And when Alija travelled, he was guarded by men who were in special services even before the war. The commander was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name of the commander, and could the counsel please turn off his microphone when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat the name of the commander you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Haris Lukovac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court where was the command post of your unit and your command post?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Just under the Presidency, about 200 metres from the Presidency, there was a school - it used to be a school for teachers - nowadays it's a high school. In that high school very close to the Presidency, we used the whole ground floor or the whole first floor, all the classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court in greater detail - because we are not all from Sarajevo - what municipality of Sarajevo was that?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I believe it is the centre municipality. I don't know exactly where the boundary lies between old town and the centre, but everybody knows the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many men did you your unit number?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Roughly - I repeat roughly - around 120, with the proviso that 70 were always engaged in the duties that I just explained. The rest were cooks, doctors, dentists, and there were some members who were not in the unit at all but there were some prominent citizens and to protect them from being mobilised by Uka or Celo or Caco, they had our ID cards as some sort of protection. And about 70 men were engaged in those tasks, and from time to time, we went to Dobrinja to hold the line together with Vikic's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you personally serve, in which buildings did you work as a security man for the members of the Presidency and Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: At first, just around the Presidency, mostly at the lower gate facing Skenderija; most of the time I was there. When Alija's apartment was shelled, then, for security reasons, they moved Alija to the building of that central bank or the national bank or whatever it's called; and from then on, I spent most of my time there or took turns between the Presidency and the bank, depending on where Alija was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1992, where was the family of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: When he moved to the bank, his wife was with him still, and there was his son Bakir and his son-in-law Jasmin. But about seven or ten days, his wife went to join their daughter in Turkey, so his son Bakir and his son-in-law Jasmin stayed there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For what reason did Mr. Izetbegovic, his son, and son-in-law live in the premises of the central bank?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, because a shell landed where his flat was, whether by accident or because it was a deliberate hit, we don't know. Anyway, he had to move -- he to move anyway and it was thought that the central bank building was safe because it was very well guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us, what did that place in the central bank where Mr. -- Alija Izetbegovic lived look like?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: About seven or ten hours, it depended on how long it took him to do certain things. Sometimes it was possible to communicate with someone else over the Motorola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just seeing on the transcript that we might not have been receiving interpretation for a part of that answer. I don't know if that was -- a full answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The microphone was switched off for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell the Court, during the period that you served in the premises of the national bank --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on, there was still the outstanding matter of the lack of interpretation from page 11, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Mr. -- you're not following the -- I don't know whether you're following the transcript, Mr. Stojanovic, but there is an issue about a couple of seconds no translation. Let me just find it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. What started as your question but seems to have moved into the answer of the witness, there was no interpretation. Mr. Stojanovic, are you able to find where it is? It's page 11, line 19. Could you repeat what you asked where the witness -- at least part of his answer was that -- well, gave some details about apparently -- or how long he was there and whether there was any communication by Motorola. Could you please repeat what you asked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. With your leave, I would request that we move into private session again so that I can mention what failed to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell the Court while you were performing your duties during that period of time, which officials, politicians, members of the military, police officials did you meet in the premises of the national bank? Which of these officials or these individuals would go to visit Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, there was Sefer Halilovic from the military and Mustafa Hajlagovic. Ismet Bajic from the police would go there; he was the chief of the municipality in the old town. Avdo Hebib would also go; Reis as well, he was there more than anyone else. More frequently than anyone else. At the beginning, for about a month or so, Stevan Kljuic would also go there. He stopped going there later. I assume did he not agree with the policies that were being pursued, but in any event he stopped going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: And there was Avdo Hebib. I didn't mention him. He was the right-hand man for everything. He was an advisor and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Reis was among the people whom you mentioned. Could you tell the Court who is Reis.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: He was the head of the Islamic Community for Bosnia and Herzegovina; that's what he was at the time. Alija was a fairly religious man, so Reis exerted a significant influence on him. Alija wouldn't do anything without first asking Reis about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When performing your duties, did you ever have an opportunity to hear the conversations that Mr. Izetbegovic had with his guests in the premises of the national bank?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, they didn't try to conceal anything from me - they had no reason to do so - so I could hear every word that was said there. That room is immediately adjacent to the other room. It was all within a circumference of 5 or 6 metres, so it was possible to always hear everything very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also provide security for Mr. Izetbegovic outside the premises of the national bank?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the building of the Presidency. I also often provided security when he went out to have a walk in the park. There was a little park in front of the Presidency. It was sheltered from shells and everything else so that it was a good place to go for a walk, and whenever he didn't have any visits or meetings in the Presidency, he would go for a walk in the park, sometimes on his own, sometimes with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you would escort Mr. Izetbegovic on such occasions, were you in a position to hear the conversations that he had with his associates who were out for a walk with him?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, I had to be able to see what was happening 2 or 3 metres away from him, never further. That was the kind of work that was involved. I had to observe the area that was about 2 or 3 metres around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From such a distance, from a distance of 2 or 3 metres, was it possible for you to hear the conversations that he was having with his associates?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the 1992 -- in 1992 and 1993, during this war-time-period, were you aware of the war-time situation in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes. You have to hear about such things. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to observe the sort of weapons, equipment, and artillery pieces that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had at its disposal in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I didn't see any big guns. I do know that -- well, initially, there weren't many weapons, the special police, the Territorial Defence had some weapons, usually small-calibre weapons. I only had 17 bullets in the clip for my automatic rifle, so there wasn't much available as far as weapons are concerned. I did see two tanks, however; everyone knows about them. UNPROFOR knows -- or knew about them too. It was between Leskici and another place. There were two tunnels. There were two tracks one track was for the traffic, and those two tanks were hiding in those two tunnels but they didn't open fire very often. But they would do on occasion. They would fire a shell or two and then retreat because they were exposed on all sides, so the Serbs could have spotted them and retaliated. So it wasn't possible for them to be very active.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time you said up until the Marsalka fell. What do you mean when you say the fall of the Marsalka,what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, when the Serbs surrendered the Marsal Tito barracks we would refer to the fall of the Marsalka to refer to the barracks that had fallen. Then there was agreement according to which they weren't allowed to carry weapons and ammunition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry and if I'm just missing then it's -- my apologies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- but I don't see that reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you referred to the witness having said "until the Marsalka fell." Where do we see that? Where did the witness say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it doesn't appear in the English interpretation, but on page 19, lines 9 to 17, it is in that portion of the transcript that he mentioned this in the B/C/S version. This is why I wanted to clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it indeed doesn't appear. Whether the witness said it or not is ... Could you tell us where exactly then it fits into -- because usually if some portions are left out, then we find a sign in the transcript that it's not complete. Could you tell us where the witness said it? Because I see two such signs, one after "I only had 17 bullets" -- well, logic requires some inventivity to put it there. And the next is "so there wasn't much available as far as weapons are concerned." And then the witness then moved on, talking about two tanks. Was it there that the witness said it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is after he said that there were not many weapons until the Marsalka fell. I think it was page 16 -- line 16, page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's -- we'll move on for the time being, and perhaps it could be verified so that we have -- do the -- does the English booth have any recollection as to anything said about Marsalka falling.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was not able to hear the witness mention Marsalka but did hear the witness mention something that appeared to be a name of the street, but a name that the interpreter did not recognise. The interpreter also notes that the witness mumbles a bit and it is not always easy to discern what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then invite him to try to clearly pronounce his words. I leave it to the parties whether we want to verify the original audio on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I asked these additional questions in order to verify the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, I would like to put the following question to you. While you were in Sarajevo, during that period of time, did you ever have an opportunity of noticing mortars being used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Every units had at least three or four mortars, those were light weapons, very mobile weapons. They said that by the post office they had two guns, but I didn't see or hear them in action. As for the mortars, yes, they all had them with the exception of our unit because we did not need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see those mobile units being used; and how did this function, if you did see them in action?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, they would go to the cross-roads, close off the cross-roads, then the mortar would be mounted on a sort of trailer; and then it would fire from the trailer for five or six minutes, and then they would flee. The cross-roads would be opened up again. The Serbs would notice where fire had come from. They would retaliate for about three times, about three times, and they would retaliate three times more strongly than necessary. And then you would have victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, how often did you see this happen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one occasion -- perhaps twice, because on one occasion, when I was with my van I had to wait for a while at a certain location -- but everyone knew about it. People discussed such things quite openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where was that when you observed it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Marin Dvor, by the cross-roads near the technical school and in the direction of the Marsal Tito barracks, towards the railway station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the underpass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question: You earlier told us about two tanks which were not frequently fired. How often you yourself did see them firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see it with my own eyes firing, but I saw them two or three times getting out of the tunnel, igniting, moving. But the people who were serving close to that location, they said, They don't have much ammunition. They fire two or three shells and then go back in. I never saw a tank fire, but I saw the tank themselves several times because they have to be started up regularly because when they stand idle for too long, they became inoperative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- one second, please. So if you say: But they didn't open fire very often, they would do so on occasion they would fire a shell or two and then retreat, that's not what you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You therefore also did not observe the retaliation fire as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you be very carefully distinguish between what you saw yourself and what, as you said, was common knowledge or knowledge of your colleagues, because you've presented it for a fact, whereas I do understand that you're telling us that you heard this from others that had happened. Would you make a clear distinction between the two always about what you saw with your own eyes and what you were told by others. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the break anyhow. Witness, we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just finish in answer to you? Wherever we were in Sarajevo, it was a maximum of 500-, 600-metre distance. You would always hear. If something big fired from this side, you would hear that it's a major weapon. And there were two tanks there so you would knew -- so you would know there was tanks. And again, when the Chetniks would fire back from Poljine, you would also hear it when it hit Kosevo hill. You would know that ten or 12 shells in one go. You couldn't miss it. It was again 500 to 600 metres away at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were never further away than 500, 600 metres when you heard a shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am talking about now, it's all in the circle Kosevo hill-Bascarsija-Presidency-Skenderija-Pofalici. It's a parameter of about 500, 600 metres. That's the circle in which I moved with corresponding visibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that Pofalici and, for example, Bascarsija are not more than 5-, 600 metres away, the one from the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but the Presidency is in the middle. So 500, 600 metres away from Pofalici, 5- or 600 metres to Bascarsija. That's what I'm trying to say. It was a very narrow circle in which the Bosniaks were able to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take break. We have to turn into ... One second, one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to allow you to leave the courtroom, we'll have the blinds down, and they'll stay down until we resume so that you can enter the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session but the curtains are still down. We wait for the witness to enter the courtroom and then the curtains will be drawn up, and we'll immediately proceed. Perhaps, meanwhile, Mr. Stojanovic, are we on track, as far as timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The curtains may be pulled up again, and we'll continue. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the next thing I would like to ask you to tell the Court is whether you had occasion to see whether the weaponry of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina included anti-aircraft guns known as PATs and PAMs?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Every units had a couple of those except our unit because we didn't need them. We had one, in fact, but we gave it to Juka Prazina and he gave us in exchange some small-arms. That was right at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina inside the city had sniper weapons?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, there were ten or 15 snipers distributed across various units, and in the end they established a platoon consisting of young men who were marksmen before the war or who are expert huntsmen and who knew these weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask you again some clarification. You said: "Every unit had a couple of those," and you were referring to PATs and PAMs. How many units were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clear one thing up. I didn't mean that every unit had snipers. PAMs and PATs are one thing and snipers another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking exclusively about PAMs and PATs. You said every units had a couple of them. How many units were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment all the units were led by former criminals: Juka Prazina, Celo Bajramovic 1, then the second Celo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you how many units you were referring to, not who was commanding them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you most men rallied around these criminal, five or six, what do I know. Some had smaller units in municipalities such as the Green Berets in Bascarsija, who did not take orders from anyone and who were active only on their own terrain. So as for the exact number of these units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, please proceed, because you're now coming to the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know the exact number of the units because every local community had its own unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you see these PAMs or PATs with all those units or is it that you heard about them having such PAMs or PATs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since I was issued with the van to deliver bread and other supplies for Biseri, I moved a lot around other units as well, so I saw a lot of it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whether every of those units, not even knowing how many units there were, had them, you can confirm that or do you say, Well, I do not fully know but I saw many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I don't know how many units there were -- maybe there were units that I don't know and didn't have those weapons. But let's say that I know a lot of units who -- which had PATs and PAMs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you know, if you have first-hand knowledge, from where did these sniper units and sniper rifles shoot from the city of Sarajevo against the positions of the enemy army?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: First of all, I must say in that special sniper unit, there were ten or 15 men. I didn't hear officially who their commander was, so I assumed they were directly under the command of Sefer Halilovic. They were made up of men from different units. Most of all, they fired from the building of the -- of the assembly which covered most of Grbavica and the Jewish cemetery along the separation line and all the way down, and the military hospital from which they shot in the direction of the Jewish cemetery with PAMs. The military hospital was not used above the fourth floor; the rest, on top, was only for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to follow domestic and foreign media coverage of the fighting around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Everyone moved around the Presidency every day, so you couldn't avoid contact with them. Not necessarily talking to them, but we had to see them and when the members of the Presidency were going into the building. Yes, there were a lot of reporters, and most of them provided rather positive coverage of the Bosniak side. If I really have to tell you this, Alija Izetbegovic gave it a lot of attention, and I believe this media war was the real defeat of the Serbian side because they did not communicate with the journalists. When some of the journalists tried to enter the Serbian part, they would be turned back. And, from what I heard, they were even mistreated a bit at these separation lines, so the journalists sided, most of them, with Izetbegovic, with us. And when they reported, they reported with quite a lot of bias. And there was an order that journalists must not miss anything, must not suffer any shortage. We provided all the -- that we could, even things that were a luxury at the time. In our language, the expression is "bird's milk."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, do you understand or read the -- any foreign language, foreign to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you never took notice yourself from any of the foreign media reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not, but at that time nobody did. At the time that I am talking about, there was no television, there was no electricity, there was no water, there was no radio, there were no newspapers. So nobody could know any of these things at that time, but later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you've answered my question, that could you not follow that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand that you said that you do not speak or understand -- read or understand any foreign language. That's missing apparently from the transcript. I didn't follow it. Witness, so if you say that journalists were always biased, it's not because you read their reports as far as the foreign media are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've been telling you, in Sarajevo nobody was able to follow foreign media at the time. There were no computers at the time - there were only starting to appear - and there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I'm asking you this because your comment on the quality of the media reporting, whereas, at the same time, you're telling us that you were not able to follow it. And even you said no one was able to follow it. Are you certain about that no one in Sarajevo noticed or observed any of the foreign media reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you're asking, but I'm telling you I didn't know it directly; but many times between them, these officials held talks in which they confirmed that the journalists were doing a good job for us. That's the point. I, myself, did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: Could you give us an example of -- you said all the foreign media were not allowed to enter the Serb-held territory. They were sent back. Are you certain that this always happened, and what's the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That happened non-stop. It didn't happen once, on one day. It happened all the time. If, for instance, a delegation tried to cross over to their side, they were turned back and they complained. These complaints passed from one instance to another. That -- that happened during two years. Every journalist would tell the same story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about the delegation, could you give us one example of where that happened, who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have misunderstood me. It's not a delegation. Crews of journalists, three or four reporters, together tried to cross the separation line; the Serbs turned them back. A couple of days later, a different group of journalists -- maybe I used the wrong word "delegation." Two or three days another group tries again. And they all say, We can't cross to the other side. They won't let us. But that I saw them crossing over, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a little follow-up. When they said they -- they can't cross over because they won't let them, were they telling you or who were they telling? Did you hear them say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the foreign journalists hung around the Presidency because there was always something happening there. People from UNPROFOR were coming all the time, and there was talk about it all the time. And if there was a shooting incident -- the journalists were, in any case, all the time around the Presidency and in small groups. They were always talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I repeat my question. Did they tell you or did you hear them say they couldn't be let in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we really have to be that precise, I heard myself - I don't know how many times - when the interpreters were talking between themselves, we were not able to cross over to the other side, we were turned back, time and time again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard the interpreters. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned units under the command of people whose names you mentioned Juko, Caco, Celo 1, and Celo 2. Could you please tell the Court where these units under the command of the said persons were stationed? Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: That can be verified very easily. Even the UNPROFOR visited them very often on their own business. One of them was even stationed in a kindergarten. Juka Prazina was at the in Kosevo hill and Skerliceva Street, which is facing the Kosevo Hospital. The little Celo, I mean Delalic -- no, Bajramovic, he had a base in a place called -- near the cathedral. The commander at Alipasino Polje was also in a kindergarten. All these units were located in kindergartens. So when the Serb artillery would start firing, the journalists would report that a kindergarten was targeted, without adding that Juka Prazina was in that kindergarten or his troops, so the report was not complete. They reported only what was convenient for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate there's a lot of general testimony going on, but I just want to express the concern that it's being offered without any time-frames which could be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps you could take that point and see whether the Chamber will be provided with more precise details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard this. Let me just ask you: When you give us such an answer about the locations of the commands of the said units, which time-period do you mean? When were these units located in kindergartens?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war until the time when I got out. Except for Juka Prazina -- because there occurred a conflict between those criminals, and Alija told them they have to make up and accept command or take their loot and take it out of the city. I'll continue later, but let me just answer this question. As long as they were in Sarajevo, they were in those buildings. You can check that anywhere. It's even in the UNPROFOR reports. The whole time they were in Sarajevo. When Juka Prazina left Sarajevo, this place where he used to be in Skerliceva Street a unit came there that later replace Biseri as the security detail of the Presidency. As far as I know, the two years that I was there, none of them moved out of those buildings, except for those who were forced to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the name of the unit of Juka Prazina and their number? Was it a brigade or a battalion?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: There were about 5.000 men with one of them and another 5.000 with Celo, the others had less, 2- or 3.000. Celo, the other Celo, had 200 or 300 men with him. I don't know if that was a battalion or what kinds of unit, but each of them pursued their own policies; so Sarajevo was very often blocked because of their internal clashes. Every now and then, Bascarsija would be blocked by one of them. They would put up barricades, and that lasted for six months, maybe even a year. And then later on, under the pressure of the international community - who insisted that they had to get rid of criminals and also because the army got stronger in the meantime and were able to deal with them together with the police - in any case, Alija called them all to the meeting, saying that they should either put themselves at the command of the army or take their loot and go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud. Judge Fluegge just announced that he would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your previous answer, Witness, you said: "It's even in the UNPROFOR reports." Did you read UNPROFOR reports yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not read those reports, but you have to bear in mind that the little bit of Sarajevo that remained in -- on lower ground, there was constant movement. You would see where the UNPROFOR was going, where our police were going. It was such a small bit of the city that when you are up and about, you always see. But the reports, I didn't read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why did you say it's even in the UNPROFOR reports, if you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, at the time, the UNPROFOR recorded everything, the whereabouts of each unit. They recorded every shell that was fired. If a military unit was somewhere, they would go, inspect, and see who was there. They had records for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and, therefore, you just conclude that it must have been reported by UNPROFOR as well. Another question: You said the international community insisted that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud. You've done that now two, three times over the last ten minutes. Next time it will have consequences. You know exactly how to consult with counsel, and full opportunity it given to you to do that, but under these conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, you said the international community insisted that these units had to get -- that the -- that the BiH had to get rid of criminals and also because the army got stronger in the meantime. How did you know what the international community requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't really understand everything you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I repeat. In one of your previous answers, you said: "And then, later on, under the pressure of the international community, who insisted that they had to get rid of criminals," and so on and so forth. What -- how do you know that the international community --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the international community [indiscernible]. At all the meetings, were they insisting on this? All the generals who arrived said that the crime had to come to an end. They exerted pressure on Alija. They wanted him to have them removed from Sarajevo or to have them integrated within military units. They would then be given ranks and therefore they would also have certain responsibilities and they would then be placed under Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you -- were you present when international generals, foreign generals, were talking to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't present. But I was present when politicians from our area would comment on the matter and say that it was perhaps time. They said that a lot of pressure was being put on them, that it was necessary to start removing the criminals. This was a subject that was constantly discussed on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you just be a little briefer in your answers. I will try to put very direct questions to you. At the time that you are now referring to, who was the commander of the 1st Corps of the ABiH in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I think it was Talijan and then Karavelic came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know someone called Jovo Divjak?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity of seeing whether he went to see Mr. Izetbegovic during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I didn't mention Divjak in my statement, but I even had personal contact with him, although very brief. I would greet him, ask him how he was, whether he was all right. He went to the Presidency quite often, but it was said that Divjak and Stjepan Sibak, a Croat, were the most competent officers in the ABiH, at least among the officers who were in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Court whether you had the opportunity during the two war-time years that you spent in Sarajevo to leave the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's been many references to a period of time and now there's a reference to the two war-time years he spent in Sarajevo. If we could just -- my impression right now is that that's 1992 and 1993, but I don't know if that's clear from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the two war-time years could you please specify them. Apparently the witness left Sarajevo, but what years did you have on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your recollection, when exactly did you work and stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: I left Sarajevo towards the end of May or in the middle of May - roughly speaking - 1992. The Biseri unit was dismantled at the time. A different unit arrived, or was to arrive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, could you please repeat the year when your unit was dismantled and when you left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: April, May -- we started in 1990, perhaps a little earlier, but according to the documents, when we were first given our official duty, it was April, May 1990 up until -- well, at the time no one really knew the dates very well apart from those who kept diaries, but it was up until 1992, May 1992. That is when I left as authorised by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show a document to you. We will then go through it together, and then I will put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the following document in the e-court system, please. 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Stojanovic, the answers are not consistent in any way. Before you show a document to the witness, could we first try to find out exactly what the witness's recollection is without looking at the documents. You said you left Sarajevo, you were talking about May, April. You sometimes mentioned 1990; at other moments, you mentioned 1992. When did you -- would you please wait for my question. When exactly did you leave Sarajevo? What month? What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May 1992 is when I left (redacted) unit. That is when I left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've answered my question. For how long did you not return, stay away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never returned again. I spent two years during the war there, and I then went to my sister's in Germany and I didn't go back to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two years you spent there, as you said. You spent two years during the war there. What were those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1980s [as interpreted] -- 1990, 1991, and half of the year 1993, from April or May 1990 till May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So just now to summarise, you were in Sarajevo between May 1990 until April/May 1992. You then left Sarajevo and -- if you would -- if would you just wait for my full summary. Then you left Sarajevo and did not return there after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do apologise - I wouldn't want to leave this unclarified. You said 1992, April/May, but it's very important for me for it to be known that it was May. Because something happened in April that, amongst other things, made me leave in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could I ask you one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want it to appear as if I left before that event in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that also mean that on from May 1992, you were not functioning anymore as a personal security detail for Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see him directly after May 1992? I think you were nodding no, but could you please confirm in words --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "no," but very softly. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to have a look at a document in e-court, 65 ter 1D05187, without it being broadcast, with your leave. 1D05187. And I would like to stress the fact that it should not be broadcast. Your Honours, we have an unofficial translation of this document into B/C/S, and I'll ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see the English on our screens as well. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document that you can see in front of you, sir - do have a look at it, it's on the screen - in relation to the question about your status, the Prosecutor was told that you were a member of the sector for the protection of buildings and for the protection of individuals in the Ministry of the Interior in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 20th of May, 1992, to the 12th of May, 1994. It says that you were a member of the reserve forces and that you had the rank of a sergeant as of the 1st of September, 1993. The name of the unit was Biseri. And during the war-time-period in ABH this unit had the duty of protecting the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you see this, sir? So today you are telling us here or, rather, on page 39, line 3, of the transcript you say that you were in this unit from May 1990 until May 1992. In this document, it's from May 1992 until the 12th of May, 1994. Can you tell us whether this document is right? Was that the two-year period that you spent in your unit, from 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did the war in Bosnia begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you should wait for the answer. You put a long question and wait for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Weber was on his feet before the answer was given. It may be that he wanted to object. You did not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No. I was just going to say what Judge Fluegge just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that we should wait for the answer. Witness, could you please -- do you still remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "1990," what do you have in mind? What happened in 1990?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, 1D05187.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I still don't think that we have [Microphone not activated] -- I still don't think we have the answer to that question about the veracity of the document, but anyway we don't object to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It follows.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And counsel said: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1388, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted, under seal. Witness, could I ask you the following. You said earlier that we should not forget that you didn't leave in April but it was in May because you remember exactly what triggered, apparently, your departure from Sarajevo. Could you tell us what that was then exactly that triggered you to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that was not in 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Markale I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then a follow-up question. What exactly was it, then, that the Markale event triggered you to leave Sarajevo? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well ... I'm still going over the dates. I'll get there. I was present when there were discussions about how Markale should be dealt with, set up. I know what took place, and I know about the number of victims, the final number of victims, so I was -- discussed it, given that this unit -- well, given that a different unit was being formed for the protection of individuals and buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you: Was that a week after Markale? Was that a month after the Markale event? Was it three months after the Markale event? Do you remember what triggered exactly you to decide to ask to ask to be allowed to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a month, roughly speaking. You must understand, it wasn't just one thing. Things accumulated, there was this, there was that. A thousand things accumulated. And then finally, if I didn't have the commander's favour I would have had to remain there, whether I wanted to or not, but I was in the commander's favour. Given everything that had accumulated -- well, I asked him, Well, will you let me go? He said I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it then approximately one month after Markale you were allowed to leave and that you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about a month, month and a half. Really, don't ask me about dates because I'll always have doubts. Whenever you mention one date, I'll have certain doubts. It was a month, month and a half, something like that; it wasn't shorter, but it wasn't really longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier you insisted that we should properly understand that it was not April but it was May - so you were insisting very much on the month - when you left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know -- well, yeah, because in April that slaughter took place at the market. If I had left in April, I wouldn't have been there when that happened, so it was May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that triggered your recollection. So you say since the Markale incident happened in April and since I left approximately one month after that, it must have been May and could not have been April. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is less correct, apart from the more correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is important is for everything to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, we are close to the time where we take a break. If you have a few questions, do not hesitate to put them to the witness; if you have a longer series of questions, then perhaps we should take the break first. One second. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be the right time to have a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, Witness. We'd like to see you back, but you should wait for a second until the curtains are down. And we will resume with the curtains down at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Once he's in, we'll draw the curtains up. Any problem with the translation? If so, could you please verify. Is it resolved, Mr. -- not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The curtains can be drawn up. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, Witness?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, if you remember, we mentioned the Markale events. My question is as follows: When performing your official security duties for Mr. Izetbegovic, did you ever have the opportunity of hearing Markale being mentioned before the incident that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Yes, Markale was discussed quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court what you personally heard about Markale.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if I may, I would like to provide a more detailed explanation because I can't simply ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We just have a -- a -- we're going into the substance, and it's not -- I don't think it's -- some things are quite that clear at this point, but I don't know what the witness is going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do we know what he is going to say. Witness, could you please answer the question. The question was what you personally heard about Markale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, if we're going to talk about Markale, we have to explain why all this was done for Markale, according to them. Sarajevo had been at war for two years, and militarily was in a weak position -- in a weaker position, and both Alija and Reis thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us what you heard about it. We don't need the background explanation. This Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about various views on what happened in Markale. We'd like to hear from you what you heard about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something I heard too. This isn't a conclusion I have drawn, but if I don't tell you about this, about what happened before Markale, about why it was necessary to do what was done at Markale, according to Izetbegovic's reasoning, Reis's reasoning, and the reasoning of others, they were expecting military intervention, and they were looking for ways of trying to bring this about. They knew - and this something that they discussed amongst themselves - that they were in no position to stand up to the Serbs. They knew that they would lose in the war. So all this is something that they did in order to provoke military intervention on the part of the international community. The first time that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are all rather sweeping statements. What meetings did you attend or where did you hear that, this from whom exactly and in the presence of -- whom were there, and then what did they exactly say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I really have to insist. It's easy for me to say these things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, I have to insist that you should answer the question. You learned apparently things about Markale. That's what I understand. Who did meet? What was said? And when was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meetings were going on all the time. It was mostly the same people around the table. Because all the major decisions were made there, not in the Presidency. And it's very likely that none in the Presidency knew about these decisions. This is not my inference. Reis and Alija were talking and saying that there is no other way for them to make the international community, to intervene militarily, but to create a major massacre. And before that, there was talk that every day we are losing 50 to 70 men without achieving any effect. Reis repeated constantly that, As you are all going to heaven anyway, it doesn't matter. They should sacrifice themselves for the right cause. They knew that they could not resist militarily, and they were looking for a way to make the international community intervene militarily. To achieve that, at the time there were very few truces. There were a couple of truces with the Serbs with a lull in shelling, so there were a lot of people in the streets and most of them were in the markets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Witness, and ask you a specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems I can continue. What did Reis Ulema say in your presence to Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: We are losing 50 or 70 men every day anyway, and nobody hears about it and nobody cares. If we lose 200 people, everybody will be outraged there will be an outcry, and maybe there will be an effect. And the purpose was to provoke a foreign military intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Izetbegovic respond to this theory from Reis that you heard?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: At first, Alija Izetbegovic was reluctant to accept this, but Reis managed to convince him very quickly that it is the right thing to do, that there is no alternative to create a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina and that every sacrifice has to be made to achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who, in your hearing, mentioned the possibility of an incident at Markale?

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Well, that idea came from Reis, and it was carried out by Sefer Halilovic and Talijan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court, please, how Sefer Halilovic and Talijan put it into practice.

utterances.speaker: GRM116
utterances.text: Whether they had help from outside or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the questions have gotten a little bit leading and they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, the last question is not, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so therefore, we leave at this moment and we'd like to hear the witness of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We -- okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's a little unclear and we've jumped, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please resume your answer. You started by saying is -- whether he had help from outside ... Would you please resume your answer from there. It is about Halilovic and Talijan putting into practice the idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant their officers. I don't know if anyone was assisting them from the officers when they were making that plan. In any case, the two of them together put forward that plan that our mortar be placed facing Spicaste Stijena, and it was known that there, in Mrkovici village, the Serbs had artillery, and they fired very often in that direction. So they decided on that axis and the angle of slope would be difficult to determine. So our fire should be directed in the direction they usually use, from Mrkovici village. Up there, there were regularly UNPROFOR officers recording how many shells landed every day. Whether those people were less careful -- in any case, there was only one UNPROFOR crew there. From their telling, it was Pakistani men, but I don't really know. And the arrangement was, when they discussed that plan, Reis and Alija agreed, and they told Sefer, Go ahead and do it. And Sefer just said, Talijan will take care of it. I think Talijan, as a former JNA officer, was an artillery man. And that's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. You said: "From their telling, it was Pakistani men," when you referred to the only one UNPROFOR crew there. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what they said there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who said that? Was it Sefer Halilovic? Was it Talijan? Was it Izetbegovic? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- please don't take my word for it. I cannot swear to it. But when he was explaining to Alija and Reis and the others the plan, how it should be carried out, I think he mentioned the Pakistani UNPROFOR men. When they were counting shells, for some reason, they could -- and he gave no further explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "he," are you talking about Talijan, or were you talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About Sefer, about Sefer, because he was the one explaining the plan; and later he said, Talijan will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were those four persons you mentioned the only ones being present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the present were Jasmin and Bakir. They were always there. They never left Alija's side, with very rare exceptions, but neither of them had any say. They were not asked for their opinion and they didn't volunteer it. They were there, but they did not participate at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these six persons the ones being present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Hebib?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the -- the rest -- he was silent. He was silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was there as well. I think that's the seventh name I hear, but I may -- I heard Izetbegovic, Reis, Halilovic, Talijan, and the two sons of Izetbegovic. And you now added Hebib. Was he present as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Sorry. My mistake. He wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a question. At which time during the day took this meeting place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again my question. At which time during the day took this meeting place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I really don't know. It was in daylight. Whether it was noon, or 3.00, or 4.00 p.m., I don't know. The meetings were going on all the time. One usually remembers what was said, but one doesn't look at the watch all the time. But it was day. And these meetings were numberless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which room did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The room in the national bank, as I described in the beginning; if I need to describe it again, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wanted to know if it was in that room. Thank you. Who was there first, at the beginning of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have no clue. I know that Alija and I came together with Reis. They were already there. Now, who arrived first, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who arrived next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We arrived last. They were already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you stay in the same room during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was always in the corridor, in the room adjacent. There is a very small corridor, 3 metres perhaps, which is a passage to that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And there, did you stay or sit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a chair I could sit down, but whether I did at that moment -- I probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not like with the others, a lot of formality. For instance, when you enter Tudjman's office, his guards were at attention. This was all more informal, less ceremony. When they would take tea for themselves, they would bring me a cup. He wasn't a stickler for procedure, that you had to remain standing. When Alija speaks to you, he treats you as an equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please describe the entrance of the room where the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please do so. No, describe it with -- describe it with your own words. Describe it with your own words -- please, when I'm speaking, don't interrupt me. Describe it with your own words because we need it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you go from the Presidency towards Bascarsija, you get to the building of the central bank, or call it national bank or whatever you will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, you obviously misunderstood me. The entrance from the corridor where you have been to the room where the meeting take place. Describe the entrance, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, but I just wanted to say that it was in a recess with a little corridor. There is a street, the main street where the tram goes, and a small side street; and when you look up that street, when you turn your back to the tram station, it's to the right. To the right, there is a large garage. Four cars were parked there in the extension behind that door where we entered. So on this side of the building, when you get into that little corridor, there is an entrance through the garage. And that corridor is about 3 metres long, and that's where I stayed. And inside there was a very big room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
